target.name: Androgen biosynthesis
target.description: Androgen biosynthesis converts cholesterol-derived precursors into testosterone and dihydrotestosterone, the hormones that drive male sexual differentiation in utero, virilisation at puberty, spermatogenesis, and much of adult sexual behaviour. Loss of steps in this route causes disorders of sex development: defects in 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 3 or in 5α-reductase type 2 leave 46,XY individuals undervirilised at birth, while excess activity underlies hyperandrogenism.

target.name: 'de novo' protein folding
target.description: Newly synthesised polypeptides emerge from the ribosome unfolded and aggregation-prone, and de novo protein folding is the chaperone-assisted process that guides them to their native tertiary structure before they can misfold or be degraded. Without it, nascent chains aggregate, the secretory pathway accumulates defective cargo, and cells mount stress responses that can end in death.

[untitled BTM module] Membrane traffic and organelle remodelling form the common thread here: newly folded cargo leaves the endoplasmic reticulum in COPII-coated vesicles built from SEC23A and SEC24B, is delivered through early endosomes marked by the tethering factor EEA1, and reaches the plasma membrane by SNARE-directed fusion, with STXBP3 acting among the Sec1/Munc18-family regulators of that step. Lipid composition and cytoskeletal geometry are managed alongside cargo flow: the inositol phosphatase SYNJ1 dephosphorylates PI(4,5)P2 to uncoat vesicles after endocytosis, TMEM30A serves as the accessory subunit that allows P4-ATPase flippases to translocate aminophospholipids across bilayers, and the microtubule-severing ATPase SPAST shapes tubules and axonal microtubule arrays.

[untitled BTM module] This grouping centres on membrane traffic through the Golgi and the machinery that buds, tethers and fuses transport vesicles, the route by which secretory and lysosomal cargo reaches its destination. Its outputs are secretion, receptor recycling and delivery of hydrolases such as cathepsin D to lysosomes; when it falters, cargo is mislocalised and organelle identity degrades.

[untitled BTM module] Membrane traffic and organelle remodelling form the common thread here: newly folded cargo leaves the endoplasmic reticulum in COPII-coated vesicles built from SEC23A and SEC24B, is delivered through early endosomes marked by the tethering factor EEA1, and reaches the plasma membrane by SNARE-directed fusion, with STXBP3 acting among the Sec1/Munc18-family regulators of that step. Lipid composition and cytoskeletal geometry are managed alongside cargo flow: the inositol phosphatase SYNJ1 dephosphorylates PI(4,5)P2 to uncoat vesicles after endocytosis, TMEM30A serves as the accessory subunit that allows P4-ATPase flippases to translocate aminophospholipids across bilayers, and the microtubule-severing ATPase SPAST shapes tubules and axonal microtubule arrays.

target.description: Hepatocyte differentiation is the route by which an unspecialized endodermal or progenitor cell acquires the identity of the liver's principal epithelial cell, the hepatocyte, which is arranged into plates and lobules and carries out most of the organ's metabolic work. target.name: allantoin metabolic process
target.description: Allantoin metabolism sits at the far end of purine catabolism, where the nitrogen-rich rings of adenine and guanine nucleotides are dismantled for disposal. The upstream steps are the ones that matter most in human tissue: cytosolic 5'-nucleotidases strip phosphate from nucleoside monophosphates, purine nucleoside phosphorylase cleaves the resulting nucleosides to free bases, and xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase performs the two oxidations that yield urate.

target.name: regulation of snRNA transcription by RNA polymerase II
target.description: Spliceosomal snRNAs such as U1 and U2 are made by RNA polymerase II from specialized promoters, and controlling how much of them is produced sets the cell's capacity for pre-mRNA splicing. Regulation of snRNA transcription by RNA polymerase II is carried out largely by a dedicated elongation complex in which ICE1 scaffolds ICE2 together with an ELL family subunit, directing polymerase activity to snRNA genes rather than to protein-coding ones and concentrating that activity at Cajal bodies.
